q: On the 787, what takeoff and landing operations are authorized on a narrow runway, and how is a narrow runway defined?
a: None. On the 787, takeoff and landing are not authorized on any narrow runway. A narrow runway is one whose nominal paved width is less than 100 ft (30 m).

src.quote: the nominal paved runway width is less than 100 ft (30 m)
src.note: The 100 ft / 30 m threshold defines a narrow runway; the 787 is flatly prohibited from takeoff and landing on one.

q: When must the cabin doors be armed relative to aircraft movement?
a: Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing. Pilots must give Flight Attendants adequate time and notice to secure the cabin for movement.

src.ref: FOM 5.1.7 — Door Arming with Passengers on Board
src.quote: Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing
src.note: Applies to every ground movement with passengers aboard, not just pushback.

q: How many start attempts constitute a successful APU start, and when is the APU considered to have failed to start?
a: The APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts. It is considered to have failed to start after three consecutive start attempt failures, or when fleet-specific procedures preclude subsequent attempts.

src.quote: an APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts
src.note: Three consecutive failures equals a failed start and drives a required Maintenance Logbook entry.

q: During which phases of flight may the crew rest facility not be occupied?
a: It must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE, and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in.

src.quote: The crew rest facility must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in
src.note: Brackets the rest facility to the cruise/enroute window; the 787 Overhead Flight Crew Rest seat, bunks, and common area likewise may not be occupied during taxi, takeoff, or landing.

q: Under what braking-action report is taxi prohibited?
a: Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by the airport or other aircraft.

src.quote: Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by airport or other aircraft
src.note: A NIL braking action report is an absolute bar to taxi.

q: For which taxi clearances is dual acknowledgment between both pilots required?
a: Runway Crossing, Hold Short, Line Up and Wait, Cleared for Takeoff, and Cleared to Land.

src.quote: Dual acknowledgment should be used for all taxi instructions between both pilots and is required for the following clearances
src.note: The listed five clearances require the transmitting pilot's readback plus a verbal confirmation from the other pilot.

q: Who must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations?
a: The Captain must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations. Restricted visibility includes any time the RVR is less than 1200.

src.quote: During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft
src.note: Restricted visibility includes dense fog, heavy precipitation, or any time RVR is less than 1200; checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set.

q: What are the standard takeoff minimums for an aircraft with two engines or less?
a: 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000.

src.quote: Defined as 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000 for aircraft having 2 engines or less
src.note: The 787, having two engines, uses this standard; when published minimums are higher and no special procedure exists, takeoff below published minimums is prohibited.

q: What is the maximum takeoff-alternate distance for the 787?

src.note: The 787's takeoff-alternate limit is 393 nm, and takeoff-alternate weather must meet destination-alternate requirements.

q: At what visibility must the Captain make the takeoff?
a: Any time the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff.

src.quote: the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff
src.note: The same 1600 RVR / 1/4 sm threshold appears in the lower-than-standard takeoff table as the Captain-required trigger.

q: On the 787, above what speed does a rejected takeoff require a return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry regardless of the reason?
a: Above 80 kts (Boeing). An RTO initiated above 80 kts requires that the flight return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason.

src.quote: requires that the flight returns to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason for the RTO
src.note: At or below the Boeing 80 kt threshold for correctable issues, no gate return is required, but brake temperature limits must still be considered; a safety report is required after any RTO.

q: At what minimum height is an initial turn after takeoff normally commenced when no turn point is procedurally defined, and what turn is exempt?
a: Normally at a minimum of 400 ft AFE, to comply with TERPS ODP criteria. A required course or heading change of less than 15 degrees initially is a non-maneuvering turn and may be commenced below 400 ft.

src.quote: an initial turn after takeoff is normally commenced at a minimum of 400 ft AFE
src.note: Applies to departure procedures lacking a defined turn point; a fleet manual or DP-specified altitude overrides the 400 ft default.

q: Within what tolerance must the two primary altimeters agree during RVSM operations, and how often are crosschecks made?
a: The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft (or a lesser value if specified in the FH/FCOM). Crosschecks between the primary altimeters and the standby are made at intervals of approximately one hour.

src.ref: FOM 5.5.6.5 — Enroute RVSM Altitude Monitoring Requirements
src.quote: The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft
src.note: RVSM airspace is FL290 to FL410 inclusive with 1000 ft vertical separation; at level-off all altimeters are set to 29.92, and use of the standby as a primary is prohibited.

q: What assigned-altitude deviation requires a Flight Crew safety report, and within what time?
a: An assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more (also an altimeter system error of 245 ft or more, or a total vertical error of 300 ft or more) requires a safety report within 24 hours. The Company must separately report altitude-keeping errors to the FAA within 72 hours.

src.quote: Assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more
src.note: 24-hour crew safety report thresholds are 300 ft assigned deviation, 245 ft altimeter system error, and 300 ft total vertical error; Company FAA reporting is within 72 hours.

q: If a pilot leaves their duty station above FL410, what is required of the remaining crewmember?
a: The remaining crewmember must put on and use their oxygen mask before the other pilot leaves the seat and continue using it until the other crewmember has returned.

src.quote: above FL410, the remaining crewmember must put on and utilize their oxygen mask
src.note: The trigger is the aircraft being above FL410 while one pilot is away from the controls.

q: For what enroute navigation performance is the 787 approved?
a: The 787 is approved for RNP-4 operations, the enroute oceanic/remote navigation capability.

src.quote: All Company aircraft are approved for RNP-4 operations
src.note: RNP-4 is the enroute oceanic/remote navigation capability the 787 carries.

q: On what maximum airspeed is holding pattern protection based?
a: A maximum of 280 KIAS / Mach 0.8, whichever is lower. Standard holding patterns are right-hand turns, and a speed reduction is begun no earlier than three minutes prior to reaching the fix.

src.quote: Holding pattern protection is based on a maximum of 280 KIAS/Mach 0.8, whichever is lower
src.note: US holding max airspeeds by altitude are 200 KIAS at/below 6000, 230 KIAS above 6000 through 14,000, and 265 KIAS above 14,000; holding fuel is calculated every 15 minutes.

q: By what height must the 787 normally be aligned with the runway for an approach to be stabilized?
a: Normally the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE. Approaches that include a 300 ft AFE runway alignment exception are indicated in the relevant airport 10-7.

src.quote: the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE
src.note: For the 787 an approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met; either crewmember may call a no-fault go-around, and do not land from an unstable approach.

q: What are the circling approach minimums?
a: 1000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility, or the charted circling minimums, whichever is greater.

src.quote: Circling minimums are 1000 ft and 3 sm visibility or charted circling minimums whichever is greater
src.note: After reaching MDA the PF keeps an identifiable portion of the runway environment in sight and maintains MDA until in a position to descend to land.

q: With only the approach lighting system in sight, below what height is descent not allowed, and what would then permit continuing?
a: With only the approach lights in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight.

src.quote: a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight
src.note: One of the 14 CFR 91.175 visual references must be distinctly visible to continue below DH/MDA; the approach light system alone is limited to 100 ft above TDZE without the red bars.

q: Within what limits must touchdown be planned, and what is the earliest allowable touchdown point from the threshold?
a: Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway, or (AS) the Latest Touchdown Point, whichever is less. The earliest planned touchdown point shall never be less than 500 ft from the runway threshold.

src.quote: Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway
src.note: A safety report is required for any touchdown less than 500 ft from the threshold or beyond the applicable distance policy.

q: What are the LAHSO weather minimums, and how do they change with a PAPI or VASI installed and operational?
a: Ceiling no less than 1500 ft and visibility no less than 5 sm. If a PAPI or VASI is installed and operational, conditions may be lowered to a ceiling no less than 1000 ft and visibility no less than 3 sm. LAHSO is prohibited on wet runways, and the tailwind on the hold short runway shall be calm (less than 3 kts).

src.quote: Ceiling of no less than 1500 ft and a visibility of no less than 5 sm. Prohibited on wet runways. The tailwind on the hold short runway shall be calm (less than 3 kts).
src.note: LAHSO also requires the aircraft not to have descended below 1000 ft AGL on final, no windshear within the previous 20 minutes, and vertical guidance (PLASI is not acceptable).

q: SCENARIO (check airman): You're the PM on a 787 visual to a wet runway. At 400 ft AFE the aircraft is fast and still drifting back toward centerline, not yet aligned. The PF says he'll 'have it by the numbers.' By 300 ft AFE it's still not aligned and airspeed is above target. What is the required action and who may take it?
a: The approach is unstable. On the 787 the aircraft must normally be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE; it is not aligned by 500 ft, so the stabilized-approach gate is busted. Do not land from an unstable approach. Either crewmember may call for a go-around under the no-fault go-around policy, so the PM calls and the crew goes around.

src.quote: Do not land from an unstable approach. ... Either crewmember may call for a go-around under Alaska Airlines "no-fault" go-around policy. ... Normally, the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE.
src.note: 500 ft AFE runway alignment is the 787 gate (300 ft AFE only where an exception is published in the 10-7); an unaligned, fast approach past the gate requires a go-around, and either pilot may call it.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): On an ILS in fog you reach DH with only the approach lighting system in sight, no red side row or terminating bars, and no other listed visual reference. The PF continues descending below 100 ft looking for the runway. What is the correct action?
a: This is a violation. With only the approach lighting system in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight. With no other 14 CFR 91.175 visual reference distinctly visible, a missed approach must be immediately executed when operating below the DH/MDA. The PF must go around, not continue.

src.quote: A missed approach must be immediately executed if any of the 14 CFR 91.175 requirements are not met when operating below the DH/MDA.
src.note: The approach light system alone permits descent only to 100 ft above TDZE; below that the red side row bars or red terminating bars, or another listed reference, must be distinctly visible or a missed approach is mandatory.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): Level at FL360 in RVSM airspace, you lose one primary altimeter and the autopilot altitude-control system flags a fault, so required RVSM equipment is no longer operating normally. Can you reset and press on, and what does the FOM require?
a: No. In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action, but a reroute or diversion may be required. Both primary altimeters and one autopilot altitude-control system must be operating normally for RVSM; the standby altimeter may not be used as a primary.

src.quote: In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required.
src.note: Required RVSM equipment includes both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and the altitude alerting system; loss of any of these drives the ATC/Dispatch coordination, and the standby altimeter is prohibited as a primary.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): Landing rollout complete, the RVR is 900 and dropping in dense fog. The First Officer offers to taxi to the gate while the Captain runs the after-landing flow. Is that acceptable, and how are checklists handled?
a: No. RVR 900 is below 1200, so this is restricted/low visibility. During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft, not the First Officer. Checklists are performed with the aircraft stopped and the parking brake set, all exterior lights except landing lights are on, and maximum attention is devoted to scanning outside while taxiing.

src.quote: During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft. ... Perform checklists with the aircraft stopped and the parking brake set.
src.note: Restricted visibility includes any time RVR is less than 1200; the Captain taxis, checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set, and no taxiing-unrelated duties are performed until stopped.

q: Rev 125: how is 787 operational/in-flight landing distance now calculated, and what safety margin applies?
a: On TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance from 50 ft above the runway threshold to touchdown. A 15% safety margin is applied to TOTAL landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance; it is calculated and varies with weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind.

src.quote: (717/787/A321/A330) Operational/In-flight landing distance calculations are based on TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance (from 50 ft above runway threshold to touchdown). A 15% safety margin is applied to total landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake configurations. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance but rather a calculated value that varies with landing conditions such as aircraft weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind.
src.note: NEW in Rev 125. The old fixed 'touchdown 1000 ft past the threshold' model is now banner-tagged (737) and no longer applies to the 787.

q: Rev 125: you are planning a 787 takeoff below RVR 500 (150 m). What governs, and what changed?
a: Use the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC, and the HGS/HUD Takeoff Briefing Card. Rev 125 extended this from 737-only to (737/787), so it now applies to you.

src.ref: FOM 5.4.4 - IFR Lower than Standard Takeoff Minimum Requirements
src.quote: (737/787) For takeoffs less than 500 RVR (150 m), see Takeoff Low Visibility Card in PRC. Table row: (737/787) <500 (150 m) - SEE HGS/HUD TAKEOFF BRIEFING CARD.
src.note: Rev 125 change. Through 124.2 this read (737) and referenced the HGS card only.

q: Rev 125: after 'Cabin Secure' and Flight Deck Door closure, what must the Flight Crew confirm before the aircraft moves?
a: All door indications closed, verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete, and, if installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) verified stowed and latched.

src.ref: FOM 5.2.20 - Cabin Safety Check Prior to Taxi or Pushback
src.quote: The Flight Crew must check all door indications to confirm they are closed and receive a verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete. If installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) must be verified stowed and latched.
src.note: The IPSB sentence is NEW in Rev 125.
